title: Love and Virtue
english: Those who have denied the truth plunder the minds of the simple, leading them astray with deceitful words and persuading them to fall into the snare of death and the trap of Hades, as it is written.
They should not add to what they know, but rather follow their own vain thoughts, not knowing what they say or about what they are speaking, because they are ignorant of the truth.

In contrast, we should stay in what we have learned, avoiding empty disputes and holding the faith in simple thoughts, as Paul says, and holding the tradition of the Church as a precious treasure, having the teachings that please God.

The path to virtue is difficult, but the command to love one's neighbor as oneself is the key to all our goodness, and it is not hard to demonstrate, for Paul, the wisest, exhorts us to owe nothing to anyone, except to love one another.

The one who loves the other has fulfilled the law, for love is the foundation of all commandments, including 'Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not covet,' as it is summed up in the word: 'Love your neighbor as yourself'.

The love of the neighbor does no evil, and it is the fulfillment of the law, for the entire word of God is enclosed in the definition of love, and all deeds that seem to have transcended the divine law have fallen outside the circles of love.

Love is present in those who ought to be admired, and it is seen through their deeds, for the one who does injustice does not love the neighbor, but the one who hates injustice loves, fulfilling the entire law, because the love that hastens to honor the things in the law brings about fulfillment, while sloth has the origin of the things accused by the law.

The virtue of love is a multifaceted one, and it is essential to examine its various aspects carefully, for as Paul so eloquently puts it, 'Love is patient, love is kind; love does not envy; love does not boast, is not puffed up, does not behave indecently, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not keep a record of wrongs, does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth'.
Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things, and it never fails, for the power of love brings a multitude of good things to our lives.

When we consider the nature of love, we see that it is patient, even in the face of our neighbor's lack of courage, and the patient person endures unreasonable things done to them by others and struggles against the things that cause pain.

For example, when the leaders of the Jewish factions commanded the holy apostles not to speak to anyone in the name of Christ, they, having disregarded this command and despite dangers hanging over them, continued to teach the crowds, urging them to be corrected and to turn away from their deception, because they did not seek their own interests, but rather the things of others, and they did not go beyond the boundary of the love of God.

As we strive for the highest point of gentleness and brotherly love, we must also consider the desire for nothing and the thorny passion of our soul, for Jesus taught us, saying, 'Give to everyone who asks you, and do not demand back from the one who takes your things'.

You marvel at the earth's ability to produce good fruits, and you praise the use of iron, which is essential for your survival, but you do not blush at the injustices you have committed, which have given you life, for you have made one thing a murderer and defiled another with the blood of the innocent.

How can you still expect the earth to produce fruits for you if you have been unjust and unmerciful, and how can you touch the bright iron, which you have perverted from its proper use and made a murderer?

For the one who has become according to the divine image, having not arranged in the logic of no one, you do not know, but you dare to strike unjustly with iron, and you do not feel, because you have been transformed into a wild beast, and having fallen into unnatural savagery, you walk in the ways of a beast.

title: Divine Judgment and the Corruption of Earthly Prosperity
english: One who thinks to ask God for the yearly gifts of the field, yet cuts no riverbank reeds and hunts no water-wandering creatures in the boat, but instead clings greedily to the tillage, defiling the God-given gift with unjust blood and granting favor to watery beasts as if they were kin to man—what hands, tell me, do you stretch out to God? And what do you say in prayer, or how do you ask for good things, when God has declared through one of the prophets: 'When you stretch forth your hands toward me, I will turn away my eyes from you, and if you multiply your prayer, I will not hear you'—for your hands are full of blood?

Yet the one who disregards any of his laws, what further concern could possibly be shown toward such a one? For the Savior says: 'Those who glorify me I will glorify, and the one who treats me as nothing shall be treated as nothing.' Therefore, suppose to him the 77.564 goose, repay its price, and bestow abundant provision upon all necessities—or, if unable to endure the yoke, endure being punished. For if it is necessary to speak further on these matters, to drink amid good things and to be filled with votive offerings, at times this very abundance for you has become the precursor of impiety. For such a thing also says the Lord of all gods: 'And they were filled to satiety, and their hearts were lifted up; on account of this I forgot them.' And truly dreadful indeed is the pleasure toward slipperiness; sufficient indeed to bring forth the progenitor of insensibility.

But bitter is the offspring of disobedience—the contempt of God. And from this contempt in our midst springs every kind of transgression. Therefore when we see you suffering this, we rightly lament and raise a prophetic voice, strengthening one another against your ungodly deeds.

'Alas, soul,' we cry, 'because the pious one who is from the earth and the one who accomplishes good among humans does not exist. All are justified in blood; each one drags down his neighbor, lifting up their hands to evil.' Upon these our transgressions we are justifiably indignant, and we are distressed, as is seen, God.

'Behold, behold the thing spoken through the prophets,' we say, 'it has come forth to us not once, but already many times.' Thus says the Lord Almighty: 'You have sowed much, and brought in little. You have eaten, and not to satiety. You have drunk, and not to drunkenness. You have clothed yourselves, and you have not been warmed by them. And the one who gathers wages has gathered them into a bag with holes.'

But besides these he says: 'You have looked for much, and they have become little. And it has been brought into the house, and I have blown them away,' says the Lord Almighty. Let us see if these things have truly happened. Let someone show the one who rejoices passing by, and I have conquered, let him seek the tearless eye, and even if he finds it, I have ceased.

You Egyptian farmers, dwelling on the land, are striving for the present, yet you only suffer the worse things from one another, and even the one who seems to conquer among you is actually the weaker, for he conquers only in what causes him pain, and his victory brings him a more prosperous misfortune from his neighbor's labors. The things you once were accustomed to boast about have long since vanished. Or perhaps not all our calamities are filled with lamentations and tears? Tell me, do we see villages lying in some places? Their earth bears the blows of hail, and through famine and lamentation they are wasted—not entirely destroyed, to be sure, and even if one were to grieve only moderately, it would still help. But the stalk is already grown and tall; let someone reap it now, and it was uttered. The one who had plowed the earth, having taken the unreserved helper, delighted in being girded for work, though perhaps even this would not satisfy him, and he often considered whether the threshing floor would be enough. But these things were merely a dream—the work of shadow and hail, not of real reaping. Yet the one who seemed already to be enjoying the good things found immediately that all was empty. Instead of stalks, wealth came as hail—much and great—and thus his hope failed. But the village neighboring this one, and bordering it, having grown accustomed to a milder anger, mourns the labors of those upon the plows, yet having cultivated a long and broad field with ease, she counts her wealth toward the present as food for satiety, but rather as the much and exceedingly giving satiety.

Your ways and your practices have brought these things upon you. This is your wickedness, because it is bitter, because it has reached to your heart. For it follows from transgressions that one ought justly to be punished, and it is necessary to weigh against our opinions the judgment.

Therefore let us cease from every impious daring. Let us beat our swords into plowshares and our spears into pruning hooks, as it is written. And as the Melodist says, 'Come, let us worship and bow down before him,' and let us weeping say, 'We have sinned, we have been lawless, we have done wrong.' For then, then God will be merciful.

And he will turn away his wrath, and the earth will again find, and with gifts according to custom will refresh us. For we do not have a high priest unable to sympathize with our lawlessness, according to the voice of Paul. But one who has been tested in likeness apart from sin.

For because it is at hand to do, I think I will need no effort to persuade anyone to be able. But also you suppose to agree with us, gathering around the measure of love toward us, and understanding the magnitude of what he endured on our account.

We who dwell in this surrounding region were all like fish caught in a net by the insatiable greed of the ruling demon. Then the Only-begotten became human, so that he might deliver us all, proclaiming release to captives and sight to the blind, just as he himself somewhere declares, and announcing this as the acceptable year of the Lord. Therefore the Only-begotten is merciful, even though the Jews, not understanding the manner of his dispensation, kept themselves from even wishing to accept him—sometimes insulting him and calling him a Samaritan, sometimes acting with shameless grief, rushing into foreign madness, and daring already to lie down.

If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do, even if you do not believe in me, believe my works. For not from those things by which as a man he appeared to those seeing was he deemed worthy to be tested concerning himself, but from those things by which God worked, not having acquired the claim of divinity, as we do, when the divine Scripture says gods; but essentially existing more with him, both truly according to nature God, and by the hereditary law of the begetter's peculiarity.
He possesses the power to do all things, not derived from another but as Lord of the powers, drawing his ability from the very substance of God and Father.

Although he became man out of love for us, we must not therefore ignore that he remains Lord of all, nor reject the Emmanuel who is God by nature, nor accuse those Jews who share our views of falsely charging him with humanity on our account.
We would not speak impiously against the one who came to be on our account, as if he were sinless because of us; nor would we worship you, since, being merely a man, you make yourself God.
For he was, and is, and will be God by nature, existing both before flesh and after flesh.

Paul will also bear witness when he writes: 'Christ yesterday and today, the same and into the ages.' You can see that he does not divide Emmanuel into two sons, nor treat him as if he were merely a naked man appearing by chance; rather, the Word who flashed forth from God and Father is granted the same divine status always.
But there is only one Son, by nature alone.

title: Christology
english: The one who became human is named Christ and Jesus because he is revealed as the Savior through his humanity.
Jesus is the name given to him due to his role in saving the people, while Christ signifies his anointing for our sake.

Before the incarnation, the Word, who is from God the Father, was not without flesh, but has become human, and is called Jesus and Christ without any doubt, as it is said about him, 'He was yesterday and today, the same and forever.'
When someone asks, 'Was Christ born in the last times?' we must respond to such questions by engaging in conversation with those who speak the truth.

For how could the one who bears the Spirit and is the steward of the Savior's mysteries have given the gift to the temple built in the last times, if he did not consider it impious to divide and separate the one and only and true Son after the incarnation?
The things that are personally and naturally proper to the Word, and before the flesh, are still attributed to him even when he has become flesh, and his divinity remains intact.
The Savior's teachings are not the result of tyrannizing the doctrines of piety or inclining to what seems simple, but rather they are the result of being instructed by his own words.

To learn more about this, one can encounter the Gospels and see what he said to Nicodemus, 'If I told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?' (John 3:12)
He also said, 'No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man' (John 3:13).
The Savior extended his teachings to the Jews, showing them the light and how they remained without a share of eternal life, not having tasted the mystical blessing.

However, to those who were disposed towards this with difficulty and had gone back, he taught again, as it is written, about the departure from here to the heavens, saying, 'Does this scandalize you? If you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?' (John 6:62)
Although he was born on earth through the Holy Virgin, according to the flesh, the Word of God descended from heaven.
The question arises as to how the Son of Man can come down from heaven and then ascend again to where he was before.
This is only possible if we understand that Christ, who is one and the same before and after the flesh, is confessed by us through an indivisible and inseparable unity of the ineffable union.

Although the flesh is earthly by nature, it is said to come down from heaven and ascend to the heavens where it was before, because Christ puts on the flesh that is his by nature, as if it were not other than himself, as far as the unity from the economy is concerned.
As the holy evangelist says, 'The Word became flesh' (John 1:14), not by changing into flesh, but by taking on human nature.

For how could the one who bears the Spirit and is the steward of the Savior's mysteries have given the gift to the temple built in the last times, if he did not consider it impious to divide and separate the one and only and true Son after the incarnation?
The depth of the mystery is acceptable by faith, for it is not investigated by curiosity, but rather wondered at by faith.
Christ, having become human, is worshiped by the holy angels, as it is written, 'And let all the angels of God worship him' (Hebrews 1:6, Psalm 97:7).
This raises a question for those who hold different opinions and separate what God has joined, thinking there are two Christs and two Sons.
How can the Word, who is from God and the Father, be called firstborn before the incarnation, if he is only-begotten?
The answer lies in the fact that Christ is both firstborn and only-begotten, and these terms are applied to him in different contexts.
As a human, he is firstborn among many brothers, but as the Word from God and the Father, he is only-begotten.
There is one God, and one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus.
Through him, we have redemption, which is the forgiveness of sins.
Christ is the image of the invisible God, and he is the firstborn of all creation.
All things were created in him, both in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, including thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers.
All things were created through him and for him, and he is before all things.
He is also the head of the body, which is the church, and he is the firstborn from the dead.

As we can see, Christ is described as having both divine and human properties, being the image of the invisible Father, the firstborn of creation, and the creator of all things, including thrones and dominions.
He is also the firstborn from the dead, which emphasizes his unique role in salvation.
The question arises as to how man, who was formed late in the world, could be considered as existing before all things.
In what way could he bear the dignity of the Creator, or be the image of the invisible God?
Furthermore, how could the statement that he is the firstborn of all creation and the firstborn from the dead apply to him, when he had not yet been created?
It is not fitting for man to create in a godlike manner, and similarly, it is alien to God to die.
However, Paul seems to attribute both of these characteristics to one and the same person, indicating that he does not recognize one Son and another, but rather one and the same Son.

The prophet Isaiah, thinking and speaking about Christ in this way, says that people will follow him and be his servants, and they will pray to him because God is in him and there is no other God besides him, saying, 'You are God, and we did not know it; you are the God of Israel, the Savior' (Isaiah 45:14-15).
You hear how they will worship him and pray to him, and that God is in him and there is no other God besides him?
They will say these things, knowing the temple in which he dwelled and the Word who dwelled in it, and they will worship not just the Word, but the one who is indivisibly compounded of both.
The Word of God dwelled in his own temple, the body taken from a woman, having a rational soul, and this body was restored to its own glory.
